Israel's Ben Gvir celebrates death penalty law by drinking wine in parliament

Israel's Ben Gvir celebrates death penalty law by drinking wine in parliament

Submitted by Mera Aladam on Tue, 03/31/2026 - 08:10
New legislation targeting Palestinian detainees has been largely decried as a violation of international law
Israel's far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir celebrates after death penalty for Palestinians gets passed into law, on 30 March 2026 (Oren Ben Hakoon/Reuters)
Off

Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir was pictured rejoicing in the passing of a controversial bill that would allow the execution of Palestinian prisoners.

The far-right minister, who has largely championed the legislation, was seen celebrating its approval by drinking and serving alcohol to members of the Israeli parliament. 

The Knesset approved the bill in its last readings on Monday with 62-48 vote in favour, despite international pleas to "abandon" the ruling. 

"This is a day of justice for the victims and a day of deterrence for our enemies. No more revolving door for terrorists, but a clear decision. Whoever chooses terrorism chooses death," Ben Gvir said, sporting the golden noose-shaped pin symbolising his campaign calling for the execution of Palestinian detainees. 

Knesset member Limor Son Har-Melech, who spearheaded the law, called the occasion a day where Israel "chose life" and said the decision is an example of "true Jewish morality".

The legislation has drawn criticism for violating the right to life and for its potentially discriminatory application, with Palestinians accused of terrorism facing execution while Jewish offenders would at most receive prison sentences for similar crimes.

The general framework of the law stipulates that anyone "who intentionally causes the death of another person with the intent to harm an Israeli citizen or resident, with the intent to end the existence of the State of Israel, shall be sentenced to death or life imprisonment".

Human rights groups and legal experts have staunchly stood against the bill, noting Israel's widespread arrests of Palestinians on broad "terrorism" charges and a surge in reports of torture and deaths in custody since the war on Gaza began.

Israel’s parliament passed a death penalty law on Monday targeting Palestinians, in a move condemned by human rights organisations.

The law now makes the death penalty the default sentence for Palestinians for killings that come under “acts of terrorism” pic.twitter.com/p3uEloeo9c

— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) March 31, 2026

Widespread condemnations have followed the ruling, with Palestinian factions, experts, NGOs and international governments slamming the bill as a violation of international law. 

The very fact that the Knesset is passing legislation pertaining to Palestinians in the occupied territories is illegal under international law. An occupying power cannot generally apply its domestic laws to occupied territories.

Leading Palestinian prisoners' groups have published a joint statement describing the Knesset as a "terrorist institution and a body that legitimises genocide".

"While the world is preoccupied with the ongoing war, Israel is proceeding with the enactment of a racist law that poses one of the most serious threats to the fate of Palestinian prisoners, in blatant and grave violation of international law," the groups said. 

"At this extremely dangerous juncture, as our people are subjected to systematic and continuous targeting, we affirm that the occupation regime has reached a level of brutality that defies description and comprehension by the international human rights system.

"This system has proven its utter inability to exert any effective pressure to halt the genocide and ethnic cleansing perpetrated against Palestinians everywhere."

'Immoral law'

A number of Israeli rights groups - including Adalah, the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI), HaMoked and Physicians for Human Rights-Israel (PHRI) - have also condemned the law, as have some opposition parties, which announced that they would petition the High Court of Justice to nullify it.

Democrat MP Gilad Kariv, a member of the Knesset National Security Committee, called the bill an "immoral law that contradicts the foundational values of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state".

'Inhumane and degrading': Israel set to approve death penalty for Palestinians

Meanwhile, the Palestinian Authority's foreign affairs ministry said the bill "ensures impunity for Israeli war criminals".

"This law constitutes, in its essence, a decision for institutionalised field execution according to racist standards, reflecting clear intentions to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity," it added. 

The Palestinian group Hamas said for its part that the new ruling "reflects the bloodthirsty nature" of Israel, exposing the "falsehood of its repeated claims to civility and adherence to human values".

On Sunday, the foreign ministers of Germany, France, Italy and the United Kingdom warned Israel that the bill could undermine its commitment to democratic principles.

Several other countries have slammed the capital punishment clause, including Ireland, the Netherlands, Egypt, Jordan and Slovenia. 

In contrast, the US has avoided criticising the bill, with a State Department spokesperson telling reporters that Washington respects Israel's "sovereign right to determine its own laws and penalties for individuals convicted of terrorism".

"We trust that any such measures will be carried out with a fair trial and respect for all applicable fair trial guarantees and protections," they added.

Damascus races to reassure Beirut as Trump pushes Syria to take on Hezbollah

Submitted by Adam Chamseddine on Sat, 06/27/2026 - 13:10
Talks of a Syrian role in Lebanon revive memories of decades of troubled relations and military occupation
US President Donald Trump shakes hands with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa at the White House in Washington on 10 November 2025 (AFP/Sana)
Off

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly suggested handing responsibility for dealing with Hezbollah to Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, reviving fears in Lebanon of renewed Syrian military involvement despite denials from Damascus.

Trump’s increasingly explicit statements have also appeared to contradict an earlier denial by US envoy to Syria Tom Barrack, who dismissed reports that Washington had pressured Damascus to send forces into Lebanon as “false and inaccurate”.

The latest remarks came on 21 June, when Trump told Fox News that he was disappointed by Israel’s failure to defeat Hezbollah without causing widespread destruction.

“They can’t do anything without knocking buildings down,” Trump said. “I’m close to giving it over to Syria.”

Trump did not explain what he meant by "giving it over", leaving it unclear whether he was referring to a Syrian military operation, political mediation, pressure on Hezbollah, tighter border controls or cooperation with the Lebanese state.

But his comments were the latest in a series of public statements indicating that Washington has considered assigning Damascus a role in dealing with the Lebanese group.

His remarks reinforced the impression that Washington sees Damascus as a potential partner in efforts to curb Hezbollah's influence in Lebanon.

US pressure denied

The issue first emerged on 17 March, when Reuters reported that Washington had encouraged Damascus to consider sending forces into eastern Lebanon to help disarm Hezbollah.

Five people briefed on the discussions told the news agency that Syria was reluctant to become involved, fearing it could be drawn into the wider regional war and inflame sectarian tensions in both Syria and Lebanon.

The proposal had initially been discussed by US and Syrian officials in 2025 and was raised again around the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February, according to the report. Barrack responded later that day with a categorical denial.

“Reporting regarding the United States encouraging Syria to send forces into Lebanon is false and inaccurate,” he wrote on X.

However, a Syrian source told Middle East Eye that a meeting was subsequently held between Sharaa and leaders of armed factions to discuss the reports.

“Those present agreed that Syria had neither the intention nor the desire to intervene militarily in Lebanon,” the source said.

A senior Lebanese source also told MEE that Beirut received several messages of reassurance that Damascus was not planning to send forces across the border.

The Syrian authorities indicated that they would seek the help of their regional allies, particularly Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Turkey, to resist US pressure for an intervention, the source said.

As pressure mounted, Sharaa sought to sidestep Washington's demands by setting conditions that would be extremely difficult for the US to meet before Syria would even consider any involvement in Lebanon, a second senior Syrian source told MEE.

Sharaa 'would love to help'

Trump first publicly suggested a Syrian role in Lebanon during an NBC Meet the Press interview on 5 June.

Calling for a more “surgical” campaign against Hezbollah, Trump said Washington could assist or “recommend Syria”.

“We can help them with that, or we can recommend Syria,” he said, praising Sharaa and adding that the Syrian president “would love to help”.

'Those present agreed that Syria had neither the intention nor the desire to intervene militarily in Lebanon'

- Syrian source

Trump's remarks stopped short of explicitly calling for Syrian forces to enter Lebanon. But during the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, on 16 June, the US president was considerably more direct.

“I suggested to Israel to let Syria take care of Hezbollah, because, to be honest with you, I think they do a better job of doing it,” he told reporters.

Trump criticised Israel for taking too long to defeat Hezbollah and for killing civilians and destroying residential buildings.

He also said Sharaa has done an “amazing job” consolidating control over Syria and “does not like” Hezbollah.

The following day, when asked whether he had discussed Hezbollah with Sharaa, Trump said “yes” but declined to say whether the Syrian president had agreed to become involved, telling reporters he would address the matter later.

The exchange indicated that Trump’s statements were not solely an abstract proposal directed at Israel, but that a possible Syrian role had been raised directly with Damascus.

Damascus rules out military role

In recent weeks, Sharaa has sought to counter the growing speculation. During a meeting with dignitaries from the Damascus countryside on 11 June, he described reports of an impending Syrian entry into Lebanon as unfounded rumours.

Ahmed Muwaffaq Zaidan, an adviser to the Syrian presidency, later told Al Arabiya that Washington had proposed Syrian involvement during the regional escalation, but that Damascus had rejected any military or security role in Lebanon.

He added that Syria supported extending the Lebanese state’s authority across the country, but through strengthening its institutions rather than deploying Syrian forces.

Sharaa addressed the matter more extensively in an interview with Al Mashhad TV on 21 June, saying Trump’s comments had been misinterpreted as suggesting Syrian forces would enter Lebanon “tomorrow morning”.

He added that Trump had expressed concern over the war and discussed how Syria could contribute to a safe and peaceful resolution, rather than calling for an invasion.

Sharaa said Syria’s priority was to end the war and Israeli bombardment, and that Damascus had discussed political, economic and social approaches with Washington.

“Our vision is based on supporting the Lebanese state once again, strengthening its institutions, and seeking a solution that everyone believes in,” he said.

“We are looking for economic channels between Lebanon and Syria, not military ones.”

Sharaa said Damascus was willing to communicate with all Lebanese parties, including Hezbollah.

Although Hezbollah’s role in Syria’s civil war had left what he described as a “deep Syrian wound”, he said he would meet its representatives if it served Lebanese and Syrian interests.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed Sharaa’s clarification, saying it had been positively received and had helped put an end to speculation over a Syrian military role in Lebanon.

The Syrian assurances have eased some of the immediate concern in Beirut. However, Trump’s repeated remarks, coupled with contradictory accounts of earlier US-Syrian discussions, have left unresolved questions over what role Washington expects Damascus to play in the future of Hezbollah and Lebanon.

How a New Jersey town has struggled to embrace Morocco’s World Cup team

How a New Jersey town has struggled to embrace Morocco’s World Cup team

Submitted by Azad Essa on Sat, 06/20/2026 - 17:32
Basking Ridge is hosting two giants of the game, but football fever has been slow to catch on its affluent 'bubble'
Morocco's players at a training session during the 2026 World Cup at the Pingry School in Basking Ridge, New Jersey, on 11 June 2026 (Mauro Pimental/AFP)
Off

Until the World Cup began in mid-June, Caroline Corley had never watched a football match.

The 22-year-old graduate of Rutgers University says her interest piqued when she learned that both Brazil and Morocco, two powerhouses of football (or soccer in the US), would use her small hometown, Basking Ridge, as their base during the opening round of the tournament.

She could hardly believe that this quiet community in central New Jersey, was set to play a part in an event of such global significance.

She watched the USA vs Paraguay game on 12 June, then the Morocco vs Brazil game the next day, and has been a convert to the beautiful game ever since.

The Moroccan team, ranked sixth in the world and number one in Africa, set up residency at the Somerset Hotel and continue to train at the local Pingree School between games.

Likewise, five-time champions Brazil are staying at The Ridge Hotel and practising at Columbia Park Training Facility in nearby Morristown. 

"Growing up in a small town - or what you think is a small town - and having something so huge coming to your town is really shocking," Caroline tells Middle East Eye. 

Both teams reportedly asked to be placed in the vicinity to allow easier travel to the stadiums during the first round as well as relative proximity to sizeable Brazilian and Moroccan communities in the tri-state area of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.

With one match remaining against Haiti on 24 June, Morocco are all but confirmed to reach the knockout stages, and if their goal difference is higher than Brazil's in the final fixture, they could even top the group and potentially remain in the region for the knockout stages.

This makes Basking Ridge a temporary base for two of the most exciting teams at this year's tournament. 

Caroline, along with sisters Anya and Fiona Cebulski, also residents of Basking Ridge, says it has been exhilarating to see the Moroccan team drive through the town with a police escort and have fans wander by to try to steal a glimpse of the team at training, or a player at a local eatery. 

"I know people have gone to watch them practice or tried to scope out where they are," says 22-year-old Fiona.

But beneath the veneer of excitement, some residents say the town has not fully embraced the moment.

They say they see how the Algerian team were welcomed in Missouri and feel as if the townfolk here could have used the opportunity to fully embrace the teams and make the town feel like an international hub, especially during a fraught political moment.

When MEE visited last Friday ahead of Morocco's fixture with Scotland, there was little signage on the streets hinting it was home to a global football festival. 

One of the town’s cafes had small decorative flags set in potted plants outside, while a banner advertising the Brazil-Morocco fixture on 13 June hung over the street.

A few minutes’ drive away at the Somerset Hotel, a lone banner welcoming "The Atlas Lions" stood outside the hotel lobby. To the casual visitor there was little to show a town hosting two of the biggest teams in the tournament. The atmosphere, as several residents and workers told MEE, was low key. 

The young women say they may know why.

'Basking Ridge bubble'

Basking Ridge is small, affluent suburban community known for its tree-lined streets, historic downtown, and sprawling suburban homes.

Though less than an hour from New York City, it has a reputation for horse farms, country estates, and as the quiet headquarters of several corporate giants, including Barnes & Noble and Verizon.

Fiona says the town of around 10,000 people, of whom four in five are white, also has a reputation for being somewhat exclusionary, which she says is known locally as the "Basking Ridge bubble".

She says the townsfolk - especially the older generations - are more conservative, and closed-minded when it comes to matters of diversity.  

In a state dominated by the Democratic Party, Bernard Township within which Basking Ridge is located, is traditionally Republican run.

'Our local community has many soccer enthusiasts'

- Ana Duarte McCarthy, Bernard Township mayor

In 2025, the township switched over to Democratic leadership for the first time in 90 years. 

During the 2024 election, most residents of the township, which includes Basking Ridge, voted for Kamala Harris, though the margin was narrow, with Donald Trump capturing 47 percent of the vote.

Fiona says the town’s political compass is part of the reason it has not come alive for the teams staying there.

Bernards Township Mayor Ana Duarte McCarthy disputes this characterisation, saying the town welcomes the teams enthusiastically.

She says the town was extremely excited and that it had organised activities during the first week of the tournament, including a watch party for the Brazil-Morocco game as well as a youth tournament that drew around 2,500 players and their families.

"Our local community has many soccer enthusiasts," McCarthy tells MEE. "It has been a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to play host to Morocco!

"Personally my husband and I saw Morocco vs Saudi Arabia in 1994, so it’s extraordinary to be in our community, at this time, 30-plus years later, as mayor, and being part of the efforts made to welcome the team to Basking Ridge." 



Hundreds of people have attended some of the training sessions at Pingry School where the Moroccan team have been training.

While the team itself may be comfortable, the students say the town has not presented itself as a welcoming hub for a diverse range of visitors.

They add that it is impossible to separate the subdued response from the wider context of the town.

Anya says debates about race, for intance, are often shoved under the carpet.

Other issues, such as the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza - a political question that has created deep fissures between younger and older generations across the United States - are not openly discussed in the town, further widening the divide. 

She says a Republican political culture has also increasingly "encroached" on local life, contributing to incidents of censorship and a limit on discussion about what are deemed to be contentious political issues of the time.

In 2023, the Bernard Township made national news, when two proposed sociology text books for Ridge High School were rejected by the local Board of Education over concerns they were too extreme and ideological on questions of race and police brutality. 

Anya was at the high school at the time when it happened.

"I think it's getting worse because of parental engagement in schools," says Anya. "They don't want their kids learning things that are different to how they they think." 

The small Muslim community in the district has previously faced sustained opposition during efforts to build the first and only mosque in Basking Ridge, which was contested for several years before eventually proceeding after a legal settlement.

As part of the resolution, the town agreed to pay $3.25m in a lawsuit brought by the Islamic Society.

In its complaint filed in court, the Islamic Society said the community had faced a barrage of abuse, saying "fliers, social media and websites denounced the mosque and were filled with anti-Muslim bigotry and references to terrorism and the 9/11 attacks".

"I think people here didn't do more to welcome the teams because they have never been the people who need to be welcomed ... they don't know what it feels to be an outsider," says Anya. 

Economic promises

Though economic opportunity is promoted as among the selling points of hosting the World Cup, it is unclear if towns, like Basking Ridge, hosting teams stand to gain much.

There is little evidence that such visibility translates into substantial or lasting economic gains for local residents and businesses.

Opinion and expectation in Bernard Township is split.

At a cafe on South Finley Avenue, a staff member wearing a football shirt says they have noticed an uptick in business since the team's arrival.

But another small business owner on the same street says he has not seen any significant increase in footfall.

At the strip mall across the street from Somerset Hotel, where the Moroccan team is staying, a hostess at a restaurant says there has been a noticeable buzz among some visiting fans, particularly teenagers eager to catch a glimpse of the players or secure an autograph.

She laughs as she recalls small groups of teenagers stopping by the restaurant to ask staff if they would be alerted should the team arrive for a meal.

Two high-school students, Eric and Michael, working through freshly baked bagels outside a cafe, tell MEE it is “cool” and “important” for a place like Basking Ridge to host a global sporting event, even if the sport is not their favourite one.

“I’m not really into soccer. I’m into UFC," says Michael with a grin.

Reflecting on the first two weeks of the World Cup, Caroline says it has given the town an opportunity to foster community and bring people together, particularly during a fraught political moment.

Given the prohibitive costs and travel hurdles for many fans - many of whom were denied entry to the United States - it felt like a rare and valuable chance to use the game to encourage dialogue and understanding between communities and neighbourhoods. 

Likewise, Anya says the Moroccan team coming to Basking Ridge should have been used as a catalyst to open the town beyond itself.

"I hope it does turn into that, but I feel like there might just be too much closed-mindedness for it to take full form," she adds.

Karim Khan dared to hold Israel to account - and that's why he was brought down

Karim Khan dared to hold Israel to account - and that's why he was brought down

Submitted by David Hearst on Mon, 07/27/2026 - 10:51
Khan's name will be linked forever to the arrest warrants against Netanyahu and Galant, which remain the most serious response the international community has made to Gaza genocide
International Criminal Court Prosecutor Karim Khan, attends a United Nations Security Council meeting in New York City on 27 January 2025 (AFP)
On

There was a revealing post in the welter of reaction that followed the all too predictable dismissal of the Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan by the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday.

It was made by Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, who warned New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Mamdani had just called the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a war criminal who should be arrested the next time he arrives on US soil, although Mamdani admitted he did not have the powers to do so.

Danon repeated the claim - that now appears to be established as fact - that Khan used the warrants against Netanyahu and his former defence minister to cover up his alleged sexual misdemeanours.

As Middle East Eye investigation made clear, Khan launched the meticulously prepared warrants six weeks before he was even aware of the allegations. 

But truth and due process were irrelevant in the 18-month campaign to remove Khan.

This included a media campaign in the Wall Street Journal, Associated Press, The Guardian and latterly CNN; private warnings by David Cameron, then foreign secretary, who told him Britain would defund the ICC and withdraw from the Rome Statute if the warrants were issued; Republican senators who told him: "Target Israel and we will target you", and being named publicly as a suspect before he had even had the chance to defend himself by the president of the Assembly of State Parties (ASP), Finland's Paivi Kaukoranta.

Danon threatened Mamdani with the same fate as Khan. "@NYCMayor Zohran Mamdani, take note: using Israel as a political weapon will not shield you from accountability," Danon posted.

A new precedent

In the past, Israel preferred to operate behind the scenes. When it attempted to pressurise Khan’s predecessor Chief Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda, it did so discreetly.

The former prosecutor described in an interview with Al Jazeera a meeting with the then Mossad chief, Yossi Cohen, in a New York hotel during a UN General Assembly meeting.

What next for the ICC and the Palestine investigation after Karim Khan's removal?
Read More »

"What was clear was that they did not want the investigations into the situation in Palestine to go on," she said. "That’s the bottom line."

Asked whether Cohen had told her Israel could "take care" of her and warned that proceeding could compromise her family's security, Bensouda replied: "He did. He did."

But this campaign to remove Khan set a new precedent. Israel claimed ownership from the start, and made no attempt to conceal from Khan himself or the outside world that it was behind these allegations.

It sent a Mossad team to The Hague, where Khan lives, to intimidate him. It passed messages through one British lawyer to Khan, although the lawyer claimed to MEE he was only speaking personally. 

Finally, Netanyahu himself "revealed" four other women were preparing to testify against Khan. This was hours before The Guardian claimed there was a second woman about to come forward.

Nothing, of course, happened.

Khan stuck to his guns and to his belief that the ICC, of all courts, would respect due process. The latter faith may have been badly misplaced.

The allegations against Khan were investigated for over a year by the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS). It made 137 findings not one of which amounted to misconduct let alone sexual misconduct.

The evidence gathered by the OIOS was then meticulously reviewed by a panel of three senior international judges appointed by the ASP. 

This judicial panel decided that the OIOS findings "do not establish misconduct or breach of duty" by Khan. They were using the same standards of evidence that the ICC itself used.

There then began a campaign by the ASP itself to sabotage the report made by the judges that they themselves had appointed. 

A kangaroo court 

Just to dwell on the last point. 

This is a court we are talking about. In it, judges are appointed for their skill in sifting through and judging evidence. 

And here was the political bureau formed of former diplomats appointed by member states deciding to overrule the legal opinion of their most senior judges, and retry the allegations in a kangaroo court all by themselves.

The campaign to remove Khan set a new precedent. Israel claimed ownership from the start, and made no attempt to conceal that it was behind these allegations

Just imagine what the response of western governments would have been if the Russian President Vladimir Putin, against whom Khan has also issued an arrest warrant, has done the same thing as Netanyahu did to pressurise member states of the  ICC.

But it was even worse than that. 

To sack Khan, the Bureau of the Assembly of State Parties, the court's governing body, had to deny him and his lawyers due process or indeed any process at all.

This included members of the bureau saying privately to the complainant and each other that Khan was finished; changing the charge on which he was to be dismissed without putting it to him; and changing voting rules.

Margareta Kassangana, a Polish diplomat and ASP vice president, met privately with Khan's accuser to discuss the case before the bureau referred the matter to the UN's OIOS in late 2024.

Another bureau member, Uganda's ambassador Mirjam Blaak, was heard telling a colleague she believed Khan "may not come back", describing the complainant in personal terms.

In my interview with him, Khan said the bureau was making things up as they went along. "It's a Khan-made process... specific to me."

In their vote to suspend Khan, the bureau found he committed "serious misconduct". The decision, seen by MEE, accused Khan of having engaged in a sexual relationship with the complainant, which was improper due to the power imbalance between them.

This allegation had never been put to Khan. He has been firstly accused of touching the complainant, then rape, but never of having a consensual sexual relationship.

The complainant’s account centred on non-consensual conduct. The bureau sacked him on the basis of a charge they had never put to him. 

Just to make sure the public hanging of their chief prosecutor would go ahead on schedule, the bureau amended the voting process, from a two-stage vote to a single vote in a manner that would deny the ASP the opportunity to make its own characterisation of the alleged misconduct.

Three camps

The campaign to remove Khan divided observers into three camps: those who believed in his innocence and the whole process was orchestrated by Israel; those who believed he was guilty and using the warrants as a cover; and a group in between who believed Khan was not a "credible prosecutor" even though his principal conduct as prosecutor was. His removal would enable the warrants he started to go ahead.

The founders of the ICC must not let it be destroyed
Read More »

This was the view of Kenneth Roth, former director of Human Rights Watch. Roth said on CNN that as the warrants were the work of a team of prosecutors, and approved by three judges in the pretrial chamber, they should go ahead.

Following the removal of Khan, the ICC’s office of the prosecutor said its work would continue without interruption. The ICC has more than a dozen active investigations in Ukraine, Darfur, Libya and Afghanistan.

But as MEE reported, the office sought in April to issue an arrest warrant for Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, and another for National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir was being prepared.

Those applications were ready before Khan went on leave in May 2025 and nothing has happened since. 

The original warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant remain in force and only judges can withdraw them. Israel has mounted a series of legal challenges and two of them are still pending.

The most important of them is that the court has no jurisdiction over its nationals since Israel is not a state party to the Rome Statute.

This is now being bounced between the Appeals Chamber and a lower chamber and a final answer could well run into 2027.

In one of the many offers to get Khan to back down, a suggestion was made to enable the chief prosecutor to "climb down from the tree". It was suggested that Khan reclassify the warrants as confidential. This would allow Israel to contest them in private.

As far as is known, all work on Israel within the ICC has been paralysed. 

Two deputy prosecutors, Nazhat Shameem Khan of Fiji and Mame Mandiaye Niang of Senegal, continue to head the office. Both deputies were sanctioned by the US for maintaining the Netanyahu and Gallant warrants after assuming leadership of the office.

Those in the forefront of the campaign to get rid of Khan are now crowing they want more scalps.

Who is next?

Chief among them is the US State Department. Its spokesman Tommy Pigott said: "Karim Khan is a quintessential example of the ICC's corruption and abuse of its supposed authority. It is good that he is gone, but he is only one small cog in this irredeemably corrupt institution. Today's outcome will have no impact on the United States' plans to dismantle the ICC."

What Karim Khan did had force. It was the most important international threat to Israel since it launched its genocide on Gaza. That is why Khan had to be gotten rid of

His boss, Marco Rubio, is on a campaign to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" as he put it.

He said: "The International Criminal Court seeks to become the unaccountable arbiter of a new global law -  empowered to prosecute and arrest our citizens at will and existentially threaten American sovereignty. We will teach the ICC the full meaning of American resolve." 

Empowered by Khan’s removal, prominent pro-Israeli lawyers are now openly threatening other targets such as Francesca Albanese, United Nations Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories.

Hillel Neuer, director of United Nations Watch, posted: "No more immunity for international officials who abuse their offices. ICC prosecutor Karim Khan sexually abused his employees. Our campaign to remove him succeeded - he's just been fired."

"You’re next, @FranceskAlbs. Your support for Hamas terrorism will have consequences."

Note the word "our".

But of course on this point Neuer was only too accurate. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar played an "active role" in the decision of member states of the ICC to dismiss Khan. 

Sa’ar oversaw "a dedicated task force and employed intensive diplomatic efforts aimed at securing Khan’s removal from office," according to Guy Azriel, diplomatic correspondent for i24 News.

Welcoming the decision, Netanyahu posted that he has spoken to Rubio about giving the ICC the coup de grace.

"He once again reaffirmed America’s determination to act forcefully against this institution - an institution that undermines justice, attacks democratic and sovereign nations, and seeks to subordinate their security to the decisions of unaccountable and corrupt officials in The Hague," Netanyahu wrote.

By joining the campaign to remove Khan, Roth has not protected the ICC or fellow human rights lawyers from this sort of abuse and attack. He has further imperilled the court and them.

A lost battle

Tellingly, on the same day of Khan’s dismissal, the UN voted to give Austrian lawyer Volker Turk another four year term as human rights chief. Israel ignored this setback and put no discernible effort into countering it.

This is because it knows that what the UN does is irrelevant. It has issued resolution after resolution, statement after statement, report after report and nothing about the occupation has changed - except for the worse.

Read More »

But what Karim Khan did had force. It was the most important international threat to Israel since it launched its genocide on Gaza. That is why Khan had to be gotten rid of. 

Israel is fighting a losing battle.

Mamdani’s video condemning Netanyahu as a war criminal ratcheted up over 200 million views. 

After Khan’s dismissal, YouGov asked American adults whether US authorities should arrest Netanyahu when he comes next. Forty six percent said yes, 28 percent no, and 25 percent were not sure.

The day after, London Mayor Sadiq Khan said that Netanyahu was a war criminal and was not welcome in London.

This is the legacy of a stubborn British prosecutor who refused to be intimidated. 

The member states of the ICC have failed the test of upholding international justice. The late Senator Lindsey Graham was right when he said the ICC was only for "Africans and thugs like Putin. It is not for democracies like Israel and United States of America".

Because this is the way the majority of its member states have behaved. 

When they came under pressure, they buckled and unfortunately that includes the Global South. When they need international justice and find it is not there, they can only look themselves in the mirror.

Whatever now happens to Khan, his name will be linked forever to the ICC arrest warrants against Netanyahu and Galant, which remain the most effective, serious and meaningful response the international community has made to the genocide in Gaza.

All the other responses are rhetorical. That is why Israel put such effort into getting rid of Khan.

Those warrants expose Israeli war crimes as never before and, for the first time ever in this conflict, make the highest office bearers in the land accountable for them.

Khan dared to stand against the mighty and powerful to pursue justice for the victims, and that will be his true legacy.

Palestinian woman delivers stillborn baby after Israeli checkpoint delay, medics say

Palestinian health workers said a woman delivered a stillborn baby in an ambulance after the vehicle was reportedly delayed by Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint in the occupied West Bank on Monday, AFP reported on Monday.

The 28-year-old woman was six months pregnant and unconscious when medics collected her from her home in the village of Qaryout, south of the city of Nablus, medic Bashar Qaryouti told AFP.

"She was suffering from very heavy bleeding and her condition was extremely critical," Qaryouti said, adding that the ambulance was heading to Rafidia hospital in Nablus via Awarta checkpoint, where the Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance.

He said Israeli soldiers at the checkpoint forced him to switch off the ambulance at gunpoint despite him explaning that the vehicle's medical equipment was being used to keep a patient alive. A nurse accompanying her was forced delivering the stillborn baby.

The bleeding woman was rushed to the hospital after waiting at the checkpoint over 30 minutes and is now in stable condition, report said. 

Reporting by AFP

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 06/10/2026 - 17:50
Critics say the actress is helping market luxury homes in Israel while Palestinians face genocide, displacement and escalating settler violence
Gwyneth Paltrow attends the 46th Annual Muse Awards at Cipriani 42nd Street in New York City, on 20 March 2026 (Theo Wargo/Getty Images/AFP)

Gwyneth Paltrow is facing massive backlash after appearing in a new advertising campaign for a luxury residential project in Israel.

The Oscar-winning actress and wellness entrepreneur is the face of a campaign for 51PARK, a development in Herzliya, Israel, by Israeli real estate group Aviv Melisron. The campaign was created by the Israeli creative agency, Why Worry, and filmed in New York.

In the advertisement, Paltrow is seen promoting the development as an aspirational luxury lifestyle project, drawing comparisons to high-end park-side residences in New York City before revealing that the destination is Herzliya.

Critics online said the campaign was particularly jarring as Israel continues its assault on Gaza, where rights groups, the United Nations and several states have accused it of committing genocide.

Over 72,900 Palestinians have been killed so far since the war on Gaza began in October 2023, with Israel violating the ceasefire, signed in October, on a daily basis. Since the ceasefire was implemented, at least 970 Palestinians have been killed, and the total number of wounded is over 3,000.

Others pointed to Israel’s war crimes in Lebanon and the ongoing forced displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, where settler violence is at an all-time high.

Gwyneth Paltrow promotes $10M penthouses in Herzliya while Gaza burns and Lebanon bleeds.

While children are buried under rubble in Gaza, while Lebanese families flee Israeli airstrikes, while Gazans starve under total blockade, she is is fronting an ad campaign for "51 Park," a… pic.twitter.com/Exl7JVKmTm

— DD Geopolitics (@DD_Geopolitics) June 9, 2026

The backlash has also focused on Herzliya's history, which was founded in 1924 by Zionist settlers on the land of the Palestinian village of al-Haram, which was part of Palestine under the Ottoman Empire. The village’s Palestinian residents were forcibly expelled in 1948 during the Nakba, when hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were driven from their homes or fled during the creation of Israel.

Herzliya was named after Theodor Herzl, the founder of modern political Zionism.

Gwyneth Paltrow is promoting 51 Park, a luxury housing project on the Herzliya seafront built on stolen land.

The site was once the Palestinian village of al-Haram, whose residents were displaced during the 1948 war.

The project is being built on land stolen from Palestinians. pic.twitter.com/uFL3LMVQRs

— 𝐌𝐚𝐥𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐦 (@Malcolm_Pal9) June 10, 2026

Many social media users accused Paltrow of helping “whitewash” Israeli settler colonialism by attaching her image to a luxury property project at a time when Palestinians are being killed, starved and displaced.

Others contrasted the campaign with Paltrow’s previous public comments on the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on southern Israel and Israeli captives.

In September 2024, following the recovery of the bodies of six Israeli captives, Paltrow shared a message of support on social media, writing: “I send you my heart. I have thought of you every day for 11 months.”

Critics said Paltrow had repeatedly amplified Israeli suffering while remaining silent on Palestinian victims, including reports by international watchdogs and rights groups documenting the torture and sexual abuse of Palestinian detainees in Israeli prisons.

Some also pointed to her previous statements about alleged sexual violence by Hamas, saying she had shown no comparable concern when Palestinians accused Israeli soldiers of sexual violence and abuse in detention.

When Gwyneth Paltrow accused Palestinians of raping Israeli hostages and she said that rape is not resistance despite all this allegations are lies while ignoring the genocide that has been taking place since 1948 https://t.co/dVuyrE4Kju pic.twitter.com/ZX1dlgbTs2

— LPC (@landpalestine) June 10, 2026

Many reports since 7 October 2023 have detailed sexual abuse and violence in Israeli prisons, with first-hand victims’ testimonies supported by reports from international organisations. 

The campaign has renewed wider criticism of celebrities who continue to partner with Israeli brands and institutions amid the genocide in Gaza.

Paltrow has also shared hostage-awareness campaigns online and spoken out about alleged sexual violence by Hamas on 7 October, claims that Middle East Eye and Al Jazeera investigations have said were not supported by evidence of systematic or mass rape.

The Israeli army, however, approved the return to reserve duty of soldiers who had been suspected of torturing and raping a Palestinian detainee.

New York Times columnist Nicholas Kristof also detailed harrowing testimonies of the rape of Palestinians by Israeli soldiers in a landmark piece published in May.

For many social media users, Paltrow’s appearance in the advertisement was not seen as a neutral commercial deal, but as a political choice.

Many also drew parallels between the Holocaust and Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with one user writing, “it’s like advertising for luxury villas in Nazi Germany during peak Holocaust.”

🇮🇳 🇺🇸 🇨🇳 **What's the purpose of the Quad?**

Group's main challenge comes from America's strategic drift, rather than from China

The Quad was once projected as the democratic world's strategic answer to China's growing assertiveness in the Indo-Pacific. It was conceived as a strategic alliance to uphold a "free and open Indo-Pacific," the vision advanced by the late Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and later adopted as a central pillar of U.S. strategy.

Today, however, the Quad is losing strategic relevance. The upcoming Quad foreign ministers meeting in New Delhi is unlikely to arrest this drift or restore momentum to a grouping that appears ever more directionless.

Increasingly, the Quad resembles a Potemkin alliance -- outwardly intact but hollow at its core.

The shift, highlighted by Trump's visit this month to Beijing, began after the president's sky-high tariffs on China prompted Beijing in April last year to halt most exports of rare-earth minerals -- critical inputs for high-tech civilian and military production. China's weaponization of its near-monopoly on rare-earth minerals forced Washington to negotiate a truce.

That accommodation has since deepened. The economic and geopolitical fallout from Trump's Iran war has further weakened his hand, including by aggravating stagflationary pressures at home. With the U.S. still dependent on China-controlled supply chains due to the failed "decoupling" strategy of Trump's first term, Washington needs a cooperative Beijing to keep inflation from spiraling and to discourage Chinese unloading of U.S. Treasury holdings, especially as U.S. borrowing rises.

The self-inflicted damage was apparent when Trump's trade war against India, in the form of 50% tariffs, killed any prospect of New Delhi hosting the Quad summit last year. India was originally slated to hold the Quad summit in 2024, but previous President Joe Biden persuaded it to host it in 2025 so that he could convene the leaders in his hometown of Wilmington in the twilight of his presidency.

If the U.S. itself is pursuing a more conciliatory approach toward Beijing, what exactly is the Quad's central strategic purpose?

Originally conceived as a balancing coalition to preserve a favorable Indo-Pacific balance of power, the Quad cannot retain strategic credibility if its leading member simultaneously seeks geopolitical accommodation with the very power the grouping was implicitly designed to counterbalance.

The Trump administration's own National Security Strategy reflects the grouping's diminished status. The Quad receives only a single passing mention in the entire document -- and even that only in relation to India. Such marginalization would have been unthinkable until 2024, when the Quad was routinely described by Washington as the cornerstone of Indo-Pacific strategy.

That is the danger now confronting the Quad. Unless its members restore strategic coherence and political purpose, the grouping risks becoming precisely what it was never meant to be: a Potemkin alliance -- impressive in appearance but increasingly hollow underneath.

Italian navy eyes Turkish Bayraktar TB3 drone for aircraft carrier Cavour

Italian navy eyes Turkish Bayraktar TB3 drone for aircraft carrier Cavour

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Mon, 03/30/2026 - 13:49
Impressed by the TB3's performance in the Baltic Sea, Italy is considering operating the armed drone from its aircraft carrier
A Turkish-made Bayraktar TB3 drone is seen on board the Turkish aircraft carrier TCG Anadolu in an undated photo (handout)
Off

The Italian navy is interested in purchasing the Turkish Bayraktar TB3 armed drone, a senior Italian military official said during a parliamentary hearing last week.

Admiral Giuseppe Berutti Bergotto, chief of staff of the Italian navy, told parliament on Tuesday that Italy had been paying particular attention to unmanned systems, including drones.

After showing footage of Baykar's Bayraktar TB3 taking off from the Turkish light aircraft carrier TCG Anadolu, Bergotto said the navy was interested in acquiring the "somewhat complex" system.

"As you know, Baykar has signed a cooperation agreement with Leonardo; therefore, the acquisition would be through Leonardo, and it can be integrated aboard the aircraft carrier Cavour," he said, referring to a partnership agreement signed last year between the Italian and Turkish defence companies that allows them to collaborate on projects such as the TB3.

"This allows both surveillance and the possibility of carrying armament," he added.

The Italian aircraft carrier Cavour, the flagship of the Italian Navy, can carry F-35 fifth-generation fighter jets capable of vertical takeoff, as well as military helicopters.

Turkey's TCG Anadolu is a similar vessel. It was initially designed to carry F-35s, but after Ankara was removed from the programme, the ship began being used to host TB3 drones instead.

Both ships are also classified as Landing Helicopter Docks (LHDs) and have been adapted to carry aerial assets.

Sources familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye that the TB3's recent performance during Nato's Steadfast Dart 2026 military exercises impressed European allies, including the Italians.

Nothing to see here: Just a Turkish armed drone TB3 taking off from Turkish light aircraft carrier TCG Anadolu during a Nato drill in Baltics and successfully hitting a target pic.twitter.com/CtmfGTYAKP

— Ragıp Soylu (@ragipsoylu) February 15, 2026

The TB3s were able to autonomously take off from and land on the TCG Anadolu in subzero temperatures, while other allied aircraft were unable to operate from ships in the Baltic Sea in February. The drones also successfully fired missiles at targets during the drill.

If completed, the sale would further validate the capabilities of the TB3, as another of Turkey's Nato allies would purchase and operate the platform.

The drone is an updated version of the well-known Bayraktar TB2, which proved highly effective during the wars in Ukraine, Libya and Syria.

The Bayraktar TB3 can carry a 280kg payload and is designed to carry more than six laser-guided munitions, primarily air-to-ground smart munitions, missiles, loitering munitions and supersonic missiles.

Indonesia became the first foreign buyer of the platform in February.

During the same hearing, Admiral Bergotto said that the navy views systems like the TB3 as "force multipliers" because they enhance both operational effectiveness and surveillance capability.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 - Over the last two months, Rerum Novarum has tracked 4,613 publicly visible military cargo and refueling aircraft flights in EUCOM and CENTCOM between May 20 and July 18. These flights involved 487 unique aircraft identifiers and averaged 76.9 flights/day across the 60-day period.

Flights over the last two months have stayed similar in total flight count.

- May 20–June 18: 2,227 flights involving 386 unique aircraft, averaging 74.2 per day.
- June 19–July 18: 2,386 flights involving 371 unique aircraft, averaging 79.5 per day.

Despite flight counts staying relatively similar, cargo aircraft flights (C-17, C-5, C-130) declined from 1,256 to 1,081 (-13.9%), while aerial refueler flights (KC-135, KC-46) increased from 971 to 1,305 (+34.4%). Aerial refueler movement went from 43.6% of flights in the first month to 54.7% in the second month.

**May 20–July 18 Activity Compared with the February 14–28 Pre-War Buildup:**

Historical data previously tracked by Rerum Novarum between February 14 and 28 (the lead-up to the war) showed 1,191 flights entering Europe and the Middle East, averaging 85 per day.

When comparing historical data to flights in the same area, May 20–June 18 averaged 74.2 flights/day (12.7% lower than pre-war). Between June 19 and July 18, 79.5 flights/day were tracked (6.4% lower than pre-war).

Despite the averages per day being lower, these flights were maintained for almost two months at 76.9 per day (9.5% below pre-war).

**Transatlantic Corridor:**

Between May 20 and July 18, 862 transatlantic crossings were made, averaging 14.4 per day and maintaining a consistent pace across the two-month period. This was made up of 409 eastbound crossings and 453 westbound crossings.

This data shows the largest change in aircraft type, with refueler crossings increasing 86% in the second month and cargo crossings decreasing 14%.

- May 20–June 18: 28 US-to-Europe and 29 Europe-to-US tanker crossings
- June 19–July 18: 38 US-to-Europe and 68 Europe-to-US tanker crossings

During February 15–April 16, tanker crossings averaged 3.8 per day. Tankers made 3.5 transatlantic crossings per day during June 19–July 18, only 7.0% below the February 15–April 16 rate.

The westbound tanker imbalance is consistent with possible scheduled aircraft rotations, which would also be supported by public reports of aircraft units leaving the Middle East this month and other units reportedly coming into the Middle East in a short time frame.

**Europe–Middle East Corridor:**

The May 20–July 18 period recorded 717 Europe–Middle East aircraft movements. Cargo flight movements in the first month started at 242 and declined to 190 in the second month (-21.5%), while tankers had increased from 124 to 161 (+29.8%).

The directional tanker figures changed from:
- May 20–June 18: 101 Europe-to-Middle East and 23 Middle East-to-Europe tanker movements
- June 19–July 18: 89 Europe-to-Middle East and 72 Middle East-to-Europe tanker movements

**Aircraft Types Observed in Europe and the Middle East over the 60 days:**
- KC-135: 1,855 flights involving 215 unique aircraft.
- KC-46: 417 flights involving 56 unique aircraft.
- C-17: 1,957 flights involving 146 unique aircraft.
- C-130: 199 flights involving 45 unique aircraft.
- C-5M: 181 flights involving 25 unique aircraft.

Two caveats apply when comparing these figures to the pre-war buildup. The February dataset covered roughly two weeks, while these span two months; a lower daily average sustained over 60 days still produces more total flights than a short spike. Also, the pre-war surge moved new units and equipment into the region for the first time. With much of that hardware now in place, these recent flights are better understood as resupply, crew rotations, and incremental reinforcements rather than an initial deployment.

Iran war wreaks havoc on global economy and could spark recession, says IMF

Iran war wreaks havoc on global economy and could spark recession, says IMF

Submitted by Rayhan Uddin on Tue, 04/14/2026 - 16:23
Middle East, emerging economies and UK particularly hit, as growth projected to fall and inflation to rise
A cargo ship leaves a berth at Qingdao port, in China’s eastern Shandong province on 14 April 2026 (AFP/CN-STR)
Off

The war on Iran has “abruptly darkened” the global economic outlook, and if it continues could trigger a worldwide recession, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned. 

In its latest World Economic Outlook, a half-yearly update, the IMF downgraded most of its growth forecasts made three months earlier.

It said that if the war is short-lived, global growth would be 3.1 percent this year. That is lower than the 3.4 percent that had been predicted for 2026 before the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, sparking weeks of war. 

The IMF said the global economy had gathered momentum, partly driven by a tech boom, only to be stopped in its tracks. 

“The global outlook has abruptly darkened following the outbreak of war,” said Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas, the IMF’s chief economist. 

“The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and serious damage to critical production facilities in a region central to global hydrocarbon supply could cause an energy crisis on an unprecedented scale.”

He said that the war had interrupted a steady growth trajectory, which had been driven by “a tech investment boom, some moderation in trade policy tensions, fiscal support in some countries, and accommodating financial conditions”.

“War in the Middle East will overwhelm these underlying forces,” Gourinchas added. 

The sharpest downgrade among G7 nations was the UK, with the IMF cutting its forecast by 0.5 percentage points, down to 0.8 percent growth. 

It downgraded its forecast for US growth in 2026 by 0.1 percentage point, to 2.3 percent. 

Many emerging markets will be hit hard, with sub-Saharan Africa downgraded by 0.3 percent down to 4.3 percent. 

The Middle East and North Africa saw the biggest downgrade, partly due to direct attacks on infrastructure and the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz. The region was downgraded 2.8 percentage points, down to 1.1 percent growth. 

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow maritime channel, around 33km at its slimmest point, between the Musandam peninsula in Oman and Iran.

It is described as the most significant oil chokepoint in the world, with around a fifth of global oil output passing through it, and a third of global liquefied natural gas (LNG). 

Few winners

Inflation globally was projected to hit 4.4 percent in 2026 - a significant increase from the 3.7 percent figure that had been previously forecasted by the IMF. That is largely driven by rising energy prices from the war. 

The conflict has seen oil prices soar above $100 a barrel, while natural gas prices have risen over 80 percent. 

The IMF set out several different best and worst case economic scenarios, based on how the war plays out. 

The worst case scenario involving a long protracted war would drag global growth down to two percent and send inflation to six percent. Such an outlook would be seen as equivalent to a worldwide recession. 

According to the IMF, global growth has only fallen below such a rate four times since 1980, most recently after the Covid-19 pandemic and the 2008 financial crisis.  

'Game on’: How Iran can exact a toll in the Strait of Hormuz
Read More »

But the best case scenario would still wreak havoc on the global outlook. 

If the war ends soon and the Strait of Hormuz is reopened, oil prices are still estimated by the IMF to increase by 21.4 percent this year. 

Energy commodity prices, which had been forecast to fall this year, would rise by 19 percent this year. This will result in higher costs for energy-intensive goods.  

“The direct effect of commodity price increases represents a textbook negative supply shock,” said Gourinchas.

“Raising the cost of all energy-intensive goods and services - including fertilisers, chemicals, food, transportation, and heating - disrupting supply chains, feeding into headline inflation, and reducing purchasing power.”

Notably, the IMF report finds that the biggest relative winner of the war appears to be Russia, whose economy is forecast to grow 1.1 percent in 2026. 

That is slightly up from 1 percent growth last year, and 0.3 percent higher than the IMF had previously forecast for this year.

Moscow has benefited from higher oil prices, and the US temporarily lifting sanctions on some Russian oil exports.
